title: Egypt's Mummified Cats Lived Hard Lives, Skulls Show
paragraphs: Egyptian cats are usually pictured as pampered, sacred companions, and their mummies by the thousand seem to confirm that status. A study of their skulls, however, paints a harsher picture of how many of the animals actually lived.

Wim Van Neer, Bea De Cupere and colleagues at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences analysed 131 mummified cat skulls from Beni Hassan, reporting in the Journal of Archaeological Science. Fourteen skulls bore injuries, and nineteen showed small perforations in the eye sockets that may be consistent with infection or nutritional stress. Roughly 86 percent of the animals were adults, against about 20 percent in earlier studies of cat mummies. Some lesions seem to have been caused by a sharp metal object and, in the authors' view, probably proved fatal. "This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies," De Cupere observed.

The researchers attribute much of the damage to overcrowding, which would inevitably have bred stress, aggression and disease. They are careful, though, not to overreach. With only skulls to examine, diagnoses remain tentative, and the motive behind the violence is open to interpretation: a fatal blow may have been the first step of mummification, whereas healed wounds show that other cats survived their injuries. It would be rash to condemn the ancient breeders on this evidence alone.

questions.q: What was surprising about the proportion of adult cats?
questions.a: About 86 percent were adults, far more than the roughly 20 percent seen in earlier studies.

questions.q: How do the authors explain much of the damage?
questions.a: They attribute it largely to overcrowding that bred stress, aggression and disease.

questions.q: Why are the diagnoses described as tentative?
questions.a: Because only skulls were available, not complete skeletons.
